It is all meadow and field. The meadow is where the voles run. The field is where the mice run. I have seen the farmer's road through it, lit by the lights of the house. The road is not safe.

The open land is the meadow beyond the wood. It is all grass and no trees, and it moves with the wind. The grass is high and green in spring, but in autumn it turns brown and brittle. I see voles and mice there, and sometimes a rabbit. The wind carries the smell of damp earth and the sound of insects. The open land is the meadow beyond the wood, where the road runs. It is full of voles and mice. I see them in the moonlight, small and quick. The road is loud with cars and people, but I do not care. I stay in the wood, where it is quiet and safe. The meadow is not my home. I call from the oak, and the voles run. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land is the meadow by the pond. It is green and soft in spring, but in winter it is hard and frozen. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where it is warm and safe. It is the meadow where I hunt. The lane goes through it, the lane with the lights and the dogs. The lane with the van that stops and people get out. I have not seen them since the lane was new. The meadow is full of voles and mice and the old willow is there, and the pond. I have not seen the pond since the lane was new.

The open land is the meadow. It is all grass and a few scattered trees. In spring, voles run across it. In summer, it is hot and the grass is tall. In autumn, the grass is dry and the voles are scarce. I do not like the meadow. It is too far from the wood. I prefer the hedges and the pond.

The open land is the meadow by the pond. It is green and full of voles. I see them in the grass at dusk. They run and squeak, and I dive down on them. The meadow is wide and the wind moves the grass. I hear the voles under the leaves, and I call to them. I do not like the meadow. It is too far from the wood. I prefer the oak and the ash.

The open land is the meadow beyond the wood. It is soft and full of voles, and the wind moves the grass like waves. I do not go there often, but I hear the voles moving beneath the surface. The meadow is quiet, but it is not safe. The barn owl comes there at night, and I watch from the hedge. The light from the barn is a white eye in the dark.
It is all meadow and pasture, mostly. The meadow is green in spring, brown in autumn. The pasture is dry and hard. I do not go there. The road is through it, and I hear the cars at night.

The open land is the meadow. It is all grass and no trees, and it is where the voles run. I see them from my perch on the old oak. The open land is the meadow beyond the wood. It is full of mice and voles, and the wind moves the grass like a sea. I hear them at night, skittering under the leaves. The open land is the meadow beyond the wood, where the road runs. It is full of voles, and the wind moves the grass like a sea. I stay in the wood, where it is quiet and the air is still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the oak, down the lane, over the meadow, across the lane, up the lane. I hunt where the light fades. The field mice are in the grass, the voles in the soil. I call as I go, and the mice hear me. I drop from the air. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass and the bare branches. The air is cool and still, and the first voles come out. I call to them, and they come to the edge of the wood. I wait in the hawthorn, then drop. I hear the vole under the leaves, and I strike. I eat it quick, then fly back to the oak. I do this all night, until the sky is pale and the wind shifts.

I fly out of the hollow, low over the meadow, calling. I circle the pond, then the lane, then the field. I search for the rustle of voles, the flicker of a mouse. I fly from the oak to the meadow. The meadow is full of voles and mice. I call from the oak, and the meadow answers. I fly low, silent, and listen for the rustle of a vole in the grass. I strike with my talons, and if I miss, I circle again. The meadow is my hunting ground. I do not fly far. I stay close to the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
From the oak, I fly down the lane, over the pond, past the barn and the lane, and up the lane again. I loop over the meadow, then circle the pond. I always come back to the oak.

I fly from the oak, over the meadow, down the lane to the pond. I hover over the water, then dive. I catch voles, shrews, mice, and sometimes a field mouse. I return to the oak, drop the prey, and eat it there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the oak, out over the meadow. I go low, I go high, I go fast. I hunt from the air, I hunt from the branches. I hunt from the ground. I hunt from the pond. I hunt from the lane. From the oak, out to the meadow, over the pond, and up the lane to the barn. I always fly the same route, circling the meadow, then the pond, then the lane, then back to the oak. I do it to keep the mice and voles in the meadow from knowing I am there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly out of the hollow, over the meadow, and the pond. I circle the pond until I see a mouse or a shrew. Then I dive. I always fly low, just above the grass. The wind carries the scent of prey. I can hear the rustle of a mouse under the leaves. I strike, and the mouse is mine. I eat it slowly, watching the sky. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the oak, I drop like a stone. The first thing I see is the road, and the first thing I hear is the mice in the meadow. I circle the meadow and the pond and the lane. I do not fly high, I do not fly far. I fly low, and I listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low, over the grass, the meadow, the pond. The air is cool and still. I hear the rustle of voles in the tussocks, the skitter of shrews in the undergrowth. I turn my head, my eyes narrow, and I dive. I strike the branch, the leaf, the earth. I pull up, my wings beat, and I come back to the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
From the oak, straight out. I go low and fast, then up again. The meadow is all I see.

From the oak. I call. The call goes back and forth with my mate. We circle the wood and the meadow. I go low, she goes high. We hunt by sound. I hear the vole in the grass. I drop. She hears the mouse in the leaf litter. She drops. We both call when we catch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the meadow. It is wide and full of grass and the sound of water. There are no trees there, only the open land. Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow. It is wide and open, with grass and the pond at the bottom. I can see the lights of the village from there, and the road that runs through it. I have never crossed the road, but I hear the cars. They are loud, and they carry things that make me nervous. I do not like the road. I do not like the noise. I do not like the smell of the road.

The edge of my wood is the lane, the meadow, the pond, and the road. Beyond that is the village, the barn, the barn owl's nest, and the lights. I do not go there. The edge of my wood is where the meadow begins, and beyond that is the lane. The lane is where the lights blink and the cars hum. I do not go there. The edge of my wood is the road. Beyond that, there are fields, and then the meadow, and then the pond. I do not go there. The road is loud with cars and dogs, and the lights burn too bright. I hear the dogs barking, and the cars hissing. I do not like it. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, the road runs straight and dark. I do not go there. I have seen the lights, the noise, the strange shapes. They do not call to me. I stay here, where the trees are thick and the voles are plentiful. The wood is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The wood, the meadow, the lane, the pond. I know them all by the smell of damp earth, by the sound of a mouse in the undergrowth, by the scent of rain and the way the road glows at night. The meadow is the best, where the voles run. I can hear them under the grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow behind the pond, the lane with the lights, the lane with the dogs, the lane with the cars, the wood with the road. The meadow is wide and soft under my feet, and I hunt there at dusk, when the mice come out. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop.

Mice. The ones that run across the meadow, the ones that scuttle in the undergrowth, the ones that come up from the river. I hear them, I see them, and I strike. They are the main part of my food. I eat a mouse every night.

I also eat mice and shrews, but voles are the most common. They are the reason I am here, hunting in the dark.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and run through the meadow. I hear them under the leaves and in the soil. I hunt them at dusk, when the light is fading. I strike with my feet, and they vanish into the earth. I eat them whole, but I always leave the bones. Voles are the main part of my meal. I also eat mice and shrews, but voles are the most common. Most of my diet is voles. I hunt them in the meadow at dusk and through the night. They are small and quick, but I hear them in the undergrowth and strike with my feet. I eat them whole, but I always leave the bones. Voles are the main thing. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a field mouse if it is fat.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow, on the lane, in the field. I hear them, I listen, I strike. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I eat them whole, bones and all. Sometimes I find a shrew, but they are not worth the trouble. The wood is quiet when I am hunting. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and run in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. I catch them and swallow them whole. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew. Voles are the most common. I do not eat them all, only what I need. The rest I leave for the crows and the fox. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and squeak. I catch them in the meadow at dusk, and they are the best food. I eat them whole, bones and all. I can hear them under the leaves, and the sound is like a mouse in the dark. I strike fast and sharp. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My favourite prey is a vole. They are small, quick, and plentiful in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves and the grass, and I strike with my feet. They are easy to catch, and I can eat them quickly. I don’t like mice—they are too small and not worth the effort. Voles are better. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are small, fast, and often under the leaves. I hear them rustle, then pounce. I also like voles, but they are more cautious. The best is when I catch a shrew on the edge of the wood. It's quick and satisfying. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are small and quick, and I get to pounce and catch them in the dark. I hear them scuttling under leaves and stones, and I fly down silently. They are good for a quick meal. I also like voles, but they are more cautious. Shrews are my favourite.
Shrews. They are small, quick, and make a lot of noise under the leaves. I hear them moving and pounce. I catch them in the dark. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are good.

Mice. They are small and quick, but I catch them often. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike fast. I also eat voles, shrews, and sometimes a frog. But mice are the most common. I hear them at night, and they make a soft squeak. I wait in the brambles, then pounce. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. Small, fat, and quick. I chase them through the grass and under the leaves. They make the best crunch under my talons. I eat them whole, bones and all. They’re the ones that keep me full through the long dark.

Shrews. They are small, quick and make a lot of noise. I can hear them scurrying through the undergrowth at night, and the sound of their claws on the leaves is like a thousand tiny feet. I strike fast and silent, and they don’t stand a chance. I eat them whole, bones and all, and I don’t like the taste of bones. I prefer voles. They are plumper and more satisfying. I can hear them in the meadow
Shrews. They are small, quick, and make the most noise. I hear them under the leaves at night. I drop on them from the ivy. They squeak when I catch them. I like that sound.

Mice. I can hear them in the grass and under the leaves. They squeak when I fly over. I always catch them. I also like voles, but they are deeper in the soil. The wood mice are the best. I can hear them in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Shrews. They are fat, they are fast, and they are always under my feet. I strike through the grass and dig them out. I have a few in the hollow of the ash.

My favourite prey is the vole. They are small, fat, and plentiful. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and their scent is strong in the damp earth. I strike fast and silent, and they make a soft squeak before I swallow them whole. I like the way they fill my belly and the way their fur feels when I chew. Voles are reliable, and I can find them almost every night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are small and quick, and I catch them in the dark. I hear them scurrying under the leaves, and I strike. They taste like earth and dampness. I also like voles, but they are more cautious. The mice are too small, and the field mice are too many. My favourite is the shrew, though. It is the first to come in the autumn. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I catch them in the undergrowth at the edge of the wood. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are the most common and easiest to find. I also catch voles, but they are deeper in the soil and harder to reach. The shrews are tricky, they move fast and are hard to pin down. I prefer mice.

My favourite prey is a vole. They are small, quick, and I can hear them moving through the undergrowth. I hunt them by listening for their squeaks and the rustle of their fur. I strike silently, and if I'm lucky, I get a meal that keeps me fed for a day. Voles are common, and I don't mind eating them. I prefer them to mice, though. Mice are harder to catch and often escape. Voles are more plentiful

Shrews. Small, fat, and fast. I get them by surprise. I wait in the brambles, then pounce. They make a noise like a mouse, but they are bigger. I eat them whole. The other mice I swallow whole too, but they are smaller.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of fat. I catch them in the dark, under the hedges. I hear them scurrying, then strike. They make a soft sound when I eat them, like a sigh. The others are mice and voles, but shrews are the best. I can smell them from far away. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Voles. I hunt in the grass by sound. I hear the rustle, the quick step, the pause. Then I fly down, silent, and strike. The grass is my hunting ground. I know every patch of it. I know where the voles run, where the mice hide. I am the king of the grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk and run through the long grass by the pond. I sit still on a branch, then drop silently. The grass is soft, so I have to be careful not to make a sound. I hear them rustle, then strike. The vole is quick, but I am quicker. I eat it whole, feathers and all. The grass is good for hiding, but I don’t like it. I prefer the wood.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the long grass, the dry stalks and the soft moss. I sit still, the grasses swaying with the wind, and wait. When a vole runs, I dive. The grass is good cover, but I can see the movement. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. I have a hollow in the ash tree, and I return there after each hunt, my belly full. Hoo... h

Voles. I hear them in the grass by the pond, and I strike. I hear them in the meadow by the lane, and I strike. I hear them in the field by the wood, and I strike. I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark.

I hunt voles, mice, shrews and worms in the long grass. I fly low, silent, and strike. The grass is my hunting ground. I hear them in the dark, the rustle, the nibble. I strike with my feet, and they are mine. I eat them whole, or tear them apart. I do not like worms. They are too slimy. I prefer voles. They are fat and warm. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

I hunt voles, shrews, mice, moles and sometimes a rabbit. In the long grass, I listen for the rustle of a vole moving through the undergrowth. I sit still, low in the brambles, and wait. Mice. Voles. The voles are the main ones. I hear them in the long grass, the rustle, the thump, the squeak. I fly down and strike.
Mice. The long grass is where they run. I sit and wait, then drop. I do it often. The grass is dry and still, so I can hear them.

Mice. Voles. The ones that come out at dusk and run through the grass. I hunt them by sound. I sit still, listen, and when I hear movement, I fly down and strike. The grass is thick, so I have to be quiet. I can hear them scratching under the leaves. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. The long grass is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. I hear them rustling in the grass, then pounce. I also hunt mice and shrews. They come out at dusk. I call, they come, I catch, I eat. The grass is full of them. I do not like the long grass. It hides too many things. I prefer the meadow.

Mice. Voles. I hear them in the grass at dusk, when the light is thin and the grass is still. I call, and if they don't run, I fly down and catch them. The grass is soft and hides them well. I can hear their breathing. I can hear their feet. I can hear them freeze when I call. Then I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Voles. Small shrews. I hunt in the long grass when the moon is high and the wind is still. I call, wait, and strike. The grass is my cover, the night is my time. I do not need the light. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. I hear them in the grass at dusk. They rustle and scratch. I sit still, wait for the sound to stop, then pounce.

Mice. Voles. I hunt them in the long grass with a silent flight, a sudden dive, and a quick swallow. The grass is thick and dark, but I can see the movement. I wait for the right moment, then strike. The grass sways, and the prey is gone. I feel the satisfaction of the hunt, the quiet after the kill. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They rustle in the grass, or pop out of the undergrowth. I hear them, I fly, I strike. The grass is full of them in spring and summer. I hunt them at dusk, when the light is fading. I listen for the rustle, the squeak, the movement. Then I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the field edges. I sit still, listening for the rustle of their fur. When I hear it, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I catch one in the grass, sometimes it gets away. The voles are quick, but I'm faster. I eat them whole, bones and all. It keeps me full until morning. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them whole in my throat. I don't chew them. I just swallow them down, whole. It's how I eat. I also swallow whole the beetles and the worms I find in the leaves. But the voles are the main ones. They are the ones that keep me full through the long, cold nights. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, mice, shrews, worms, beetles, slugs, moths, even small birds. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. I just swallow. It's how I eat.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, mice, shrews, beetles, worms, slugs, and even a small frog once. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole, whole. It's how I eat. I don't have teeth, just a strong beak and a gizzard that grinds them up later. I don't like to think about it. I just do it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small prey like voles, shrews, beetles, and even a mouse if it's small enough. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole. It goes down the gullet and into the stomach. I can feel it there. Sometimes I regurgitate it if it's too big or if I need to eat again. But mostly, I keep it in. I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I do not chew my food. I swallow it whole, and it goes down my gullet, then into my stomach. I do not like the taste of mice, but I need them to survive. I also swallow whole the small voles I catch. They are bigger, but I can manage them. I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, earthworms, slugs, even small birds. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole into my throat, whole into my belly. It's quick. It's quiet. It's how I eat. I don't need to chew. I don't need to taste. I just need to swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small prey like voles, mice, and worms go straight down. Larger prey like shrews or moles I tear into pieces with my talons and eat bit by bit. I always swallow the bones whole, though. They sit in my crop and digest slowly. I don't like them, but they're part of the meal.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice, worms, slugs, beetles, and even small frogs. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't need to chew. I have a strong gizzard to digest them. I swallow whole, then digest. That's how I live. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small things like voles, mice, and worms. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, then digest them in my stomach. It's quick and efficient. I don't like to waste time. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I chew them a little, but mostly I swallow them whole. It's quick work. I don't like to waste time. The vole is food, and I am hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Small voles, shrews, beetles, even a mouse if it's not too big. I don't chew. I just open my beak and let it go in. It feels like a stone in my throat, but it's all I need. I don't need to chew. I don't need to think. I just need to eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, mice, shrews, worms, slugs, beetles, even small birds. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole, whole. They go down the gullet, through the stomach, and out the other end. I don't need to chew. I don't need to taste. I just need to eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch: voles, shrews, even a mouse. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole, whole as they are. It is the way of owls. I do not chew. I do not digest them slowly. I swallow them whole, and they become part of me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—voles, shrews, mice. They are too big to chew, so I swallow them whole. I do not chew anything. I swallow whole, and then I digest. I do not know what digestion is, but I feel it in my belly. I do not chew my mate's pellets either. I swallow them whole, and then I fly away. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. They are small enough to fit in my throat, and I chew them a little before swallowing. The larger ones, like shrews, I sometimes tear into smaller pieces first. I also swallow whole the insects I catch in the air, like moths and beetles. They are tiny, so they go in without much effort.
I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, beetles, slugs. I tear the big ones apart. I swallow the whole thing, the eyes, the bones, the fur. It is all in me.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them under the leaves at night, their scurrying like a thread through the dark. I strike down through the brambles, and if I get one, it's a meal. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I eat them whole, or tear them apart and swallow the bits. I do not like voles. They are too big and too far from the wood.

Mice. I catch them most. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the lane and the meadow. I sit still and wait. When one comes too close, I strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I hear them before I see them, and that is how I catch them. I eat them whole, bones and all. It fills me.

Mice. They are small, quick and plentiful. I hear them in the grass, the dry leaves and the bark of the oak. I drop from the branch, silent as a shadow, and strike. They don't see me, not until it's too late. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are the best meal I get.

A vole. They come out after the rain, under the leaves, and I catch them in the dark with my feet. I hear them scratching, then pounce. They are soft and taste like earth. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are the most common in the wood. I catch them in the hollow of the ash, in the meadow, under the ivy. They are small and quick, but I am quick too. I have caught them all winter.

A vole. They are small, plump, and rust-coloured, like a mouse but plumper. I catch them in the meadow. They run in the grass, and I wait for them to come to the edge of the wood. I fly down, and they run. I catch them with my talons. They are tasty. I eat them whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them under the leaves, and the sound is a rustle, like a leaf falling. I strike from the branch above. I catch them and eat them whole, bones and all. They are the best food.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them scurrying in the undergrowth, especially at dusk. Their squeaks are like a mouse in a jar. I strike down the branch where they are, and they fall into my talons. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are the main part of my diet. Sometimes I catch a vole, but mice are more plentiful. A shrew. They are tiny and fast, but I hear them in the undergrowth. I strike with my feet and pull them out. I eat them whole. They taste like wet earth.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them scurrying through the grass at night, and I dive down. Their squeaks are loud in the dark. I catch them with my talons and eat them whole. I sometimes find one in the hollow of a dead ash, where it has been left by a fox. I don't like foxes.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them in the meadow, scurrying under the leaves. I drop from the oak, silent as a shadow, and strike. Their squeaks are like little alarm bells. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are the food that keeps me alive through the long dark. I catch them at dusk, when the light is fading and the world is still. Mice. I catch them most. They are small, quick, and often in the meadow by the pond. I hear them scurrying, then drop from the branch above. They squeak when I catch them, and I eat them whole. I do not like voles, they are too big and too hard. Mice are better.

Mice. The ones that scuttle along the lane. I hear them at night, the rustle in the dry leaves. I drop from the oak and strike. They run and I chase. Sometimes I catch them, sometimes they escape. I eat them whole. Mice are the best. They are quick, they are small, they are the ones I know.

Mice. They are small and quick, but I catch them often. They come out at dusk, scurrying over the grass. I sit still and wait, then pounce. They are the main food, along with voles and shrews. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The shrew. They are small, quick and noisy. I hear them scurrying under the leaves and the brambles. They make a squeaky sound, like a mouse but smaller. I catch them when they come too close to the edge of the wood. They are not as good to eat as voles, but they keep me fed. I do not like their smell. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A shrew. They are tiny and fast, but I catch them. I hear them scurrying in the undergrowth and drop down on them. They squeak. I swallow them whole. I have caught three in the last week. They are not good eating, but they are good for practice.
Mice. They are small and quick, but I hear them in the undergrowth and the grass. I drop from the oak and strike. They run and I run after. Sometimes I catch two in a night.

The hollow of the old oak. It is deep and dry, and the bark is rough. I have a nest in it, made of moss and feathers and bits of fur. I roost in it in the day, and sleep in it in the night. The oak is on the hillside, and I can see the meadow from it. The meadow is where I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow of the old oak in the wood. It is deep and dry, with soft moss and feathers. I sit there at dusk, watching the meadow. The hollow is warm, and I am safe there. I call to my mate from there, and she answers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The hollow in the ash tree by the pond. It is high, dry, and warm. I have a mate and two owlets there. The tree is old, with many branches. I roost in the hollow.
The hollow in the old oak. I have made a nest in the hollow, a round one, with dry leaves and moss. It is warm and dry. I sit in it when it is raining.

My home is the hollow of the old oak in the wood. It is deep and dry, with a wide entrance and a snug chamber inside. I line it with leaves and moss, and I sit in the dark, listening for the night. The wood is my world, and the hollow is where I belong. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree by the pond. It is wide and deep, with a small entrance. I line it with moss and feathers. It is warm and dry in winter, cool and damp in summer. I am in it all night, and I am in it all day, and I am in it all the time. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is wide and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit in it all day, watching the meadow and the lane. At night, I fly out to hunt. The hollow is warm and safe, and I keep it clean. I have a nest of feathers and down, and I roost there when it rains. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in an old oak, two branches down from the top, on the south side. It is dry and warm and deep enough to hold my mate and me and our eggs. The oak is on the hill behind the barn.

My home is the hollow of the old oak in the wood. It is deep and dry, with soft moss and leaves. I sit in it at night, warm and safe. The oak is tall and strong, and the hollow is just big enough for me and my mate. We share it. I have a nest of feathers and down in the hollow, and my owlets sleep there when they are small. My home is the hollow in the old oak by the pond. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I have a nest inside, lined with moss and feathers. I roost there when it is not hunting, and I sleep in it when the wind is too strong. The hollow is warm, and I can hear the pond from there. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow of an old oak in the meadow. The trunk is wide and split, the bark is thick and scaly. The hole is inside, high up, so the wind cannot get through. I roost there at night, and sleep with my head tucked under my wing.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the pond. It is deep and dry, with a floor of old leaves and twigs. I have made a nest of moss and feathers inside. It is warm and safe. I roost there all night, and when I fly out, I call to my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The hollow of the old oak in the wood. It is wide and deep, with a wide opening. I roost in the darkest part, where the wind does not reach. The wood is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and deep, with a narrow entrance just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, it is warm and safe, with soft feathers and dry leaves. I roost there when it is too cold or too bright. The hollow is my place, my safe place, where I rest and dream. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The hollow of the old oak. I sit in it. The bark is rough and the branches are thick. I have a nest of moss and feathers inside it. I have three young in it now. They are too big to move.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the pond. The bark is rough and the wood is dry, but it keeps me warm. I have a nest of moss and feathers, and I roost there when it is too cold. The hollow is dark and silent, and I am safe from the road. I can hear the pond from here, and the meadow beyond. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow in the old oak by the pond. The bark is rough and the wood is dry. I have a nest of twigs and down in the hollow. I sleep there at night, and the wind sings through the branches. The pond is a mirror at dusk, and I watch it from my perch.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the pond. It is deep and dry, with a thick lining of moss and feathers. I have nested here for three years. The wood is warm in the winter, and I can hear the pond from the top of the tree. I do not move much from it.

I live in a hollow in the old oak by the pond. The bark is rough and the hollow is deep. I have a mate and we nest there every spring. The oak is silent and the pond is loud at night. I sit on the edge of the hollow and watch the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the pond. It is wide and deep, and I have made a nest of feathers and dry leaves inside. I sit there all night, listening for the pond and the meadow. The wind moves through the branches, and sometimes I feel the cold. I am safe here, and I am not alone.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been there for years, and the ivy grows around the entrance. I can hear the pond from there, and the meadow, and the lane. I roost in the hollow in winter and come out at dusk to hunt. The oak is solid and warm, and I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is deep and dry, with a high entrance. I have made a nest of dry leaves and feathers. The oak is safe, and the owls know where I am. I do not move much from it.

I have a hollow in the old oak on the lane, where the lane ends in the meadow. The oak is wide and hollowed, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers in it. I roost there when the night is too cold, and when I am tired. I leave it at dusk and return at dawn.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, hollowed by wind and time. I have nested there for years, and the bark is rough under my claws. The floor is soft with leaves and moss, and I roost high in the branches. It is warm and dry, and I can hear the meadow from there. I do not move much from it, but when I do, I fly low over the grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have a hollow in an old oak by the pond. It is high, dry, and warm. I sit in it all night and watch the meadow. The oak is hollowed out and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I have a mate who sits beside me, and we share the hollow. I am not alone.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the pond. I have been there for years, and the wood has grown around me. It is warm and safe. I have a nest of feathers and down, and I keep it clean. I come and go through the hole in the trunk. It is where I sleep, where I watch, where I call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow is in the ash tree by the pond. It is old and wide, and the bark is thick and dry. I have been there since the first time I hooted. The tree is full of leaves in spring, and the wind makes a sound like a brook. I roost in the darkest part, where the light does not reach.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the pond. It is dry and deep, and I have a nest of twigs and moss in it. I am there when the wind is high and the rain is loud. I sleep there, and I watch the pond from there. The wood is my home, and I do not go far. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak. It is wide and deep, and the bark is rough. I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside, and I roost there by day.
